transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-05
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Redwood), Samir Patel (Bluefield ML Eng), Rachel Gomez (Bluefield Head of Data), Liam O'Connor (Bluefield Security), Nadia Ruiz (Bluefield Product), Speaker 6

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be noisy):
- Reviewed current KV/prefix cache hit rates and discovered drift in prompt families causing lower-than-expected reuse.
- Discussed eviction policies and TTLs; tested LRU vs TTL-first; found TTL-first reduces stale prefixes but increases cold-start tokens in some flows.
- Agreed to run controlled experiments on a isolated Dedicated test slot to measure latency/cost tradeoffs with different eviction thresholds and prefetch windows.
- Next steps: traces, updated docs, test slot, baseline run scheduled.

Topics: prefix cache hit rates, prompt reuse strategy, eviction policy (LRU vs TTL), prefetch & hot-key detection, instrumentation, compliance notes on traces

Action items (listed above)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: All right, good afternoon uh Bluefield team, thanks for making time. Jordan from Redwood here, AE. Uh we've got Priya and Maya on from the engineering side. How's everyone?
[00:14] Samir Patel: Hey Jordan, doing well. Quick note, we've pulled some fresh logs from the pilot cluster overnight. Looks like hit rates are lower than we expected on the treatment group.
[00:23] Priya Nair: Cool, can you share ballpark numbers, Samir? Is that prefix cache or K-V cache? Sometimes the telemetry mixes them.
[00:33] Samir Patel: Yeah, primarily prefix-level reuse — so the prefix cache hit for user prompts is about 42% for the primary route, where we were projecting 65% by week two. Token-level KV hits are about 58%. There's also a long tail of low-frequency prompts.
[00:48] Rachel Gomez: To add, many of our prompts have dynamic placeholders we replaced client-side, so same intent but different surface tokens. That might be breaking prefix match heuristics.
[00:59] Maya Chen: That's exactly the kind of prompt engineering and reuse strategy we wanted to surface. One pattern we recommend is canonicalization — reduce surface variability before sending. Did you try our lightweight canonicalizer?
[01:12] Samir Patel: We ran the basic rewrites but not the full canonicalizer, no. Some of the placeholder tokenization is done in the UI and hard to change quickly.
[01:22] Priya Nair: Okay, so two orthogonal issues — canonicalization to increase logical reuse, and eviction/TTL tuning to avoid keeping stale prefixes. We saw in other pilots that TTL-first eviction prevented size blow-up, but it sometimes lowered prefix-hit for mid-frequency queries.
[01:38] Liam O'Connor: From security, we need to ensure traces we share strip PHI/PII. We can't send raw prompts with patient identifiers.
[01:46] Jordan Lee: Definitely, we'll add that to the export checklist. Samir, can you produce a 48-hour trace with token-level anonymization? If not, we'll help with a sanitization script.
[01:57] Samir Patel: Yup, we can do anonymization. We'll need an example script from Redwood to keep formats consistent.
[02:05] Jordan Lee: We'll include that in the doc. Quick question: are you using streaming responses in production routes? Streaming affects prefix reuse because partial outputs can change the cache key.
[02:17] Nadia Ruiz: We are using streaming for the clinician assistant flow but not for batch reports. Clinician flow is high-value and latency-sensitive.
[02:26] Priya Nair: Right, streaming complicates continuous KV caching due to incremental token emission. For streaming, we often prefer shorter TTLs but more aggressive prefix normalization.
[02:36] Speaker 6: Sorry, could someone define prefix cache vs KV cache one more time for our PM?
[02:42] Maya Chen: Sure — prefix cache stores previous full-token sequences for common prompt prefixes so the model can resume generation with fewer compute cycles. KV cache (key-value cache) is the model's internal attention cache used per request for decoding speed. They interact but are different.
[02:56] Samir Patel: We also noticed a spike in cost when the hit rate dropped — reason being more tokens generated from scratch. We need to evaluate cost impact.
[03:06] Priya Nair: For cost math, can you share per-token cost from your trial? We can map hit rate to token savings.
[03:12] Rachel Gomez: We'll pull that.
[03:16] Jordan Lee: Cool. Okay, on eviction strategies — we've run three configs in other pilots: LRU-heavy, TTL-first (short TTLs, periodic sweep), and adaptive hot-key retention (keep top-K prefixes per user). We can run those against your workload.
[03:30] Samir Patel: We tried LRU-heavy for a week but saw thrash — high churn for mid-frequency prompts. TTL-first seemed promising but we didn't tune TTL durations.
[03:39] Priya Nair: TTL tuning is sensitive. For clinician flows, a 30–60 second TTL may be too short if sessions are spaced. For conversational flows, 5–15s TTL can help. We need to look at inter-arrival distributions.
[03:52] Jordan Lee: Do you have session gap stats? median and p95?
[03:56] Samir Patel: Median inter-request is around 12s for clinician session, p95 is 420s. So there's a long tail.
[04:04] Maya Chen: That explains why TTL-first erased many useful prefixes; p95 >> median. An adaptive TTL or per-user top-K is better here.
[04:13] Nadia Ruiz: What's the impact of increasing top-K? More memory, right?
[04:17] Priya Nair: Yes. Top-K retention trades memory for reuse. We recommend calculating expected memory per slot: average prefix size * top-K * number of active users. We'll run numbers after we get traces.
[04:29] Jordan Lee: For the pilot, propose two controlled experiments: one with adaptive top-K (K=5 per user + LRU background), one with TTL-adaptive (median-based TTL plus jitter). Run each for 48h on an isolated slot and measure prefix hit, token delta, latency P50/P95, and cost.
[04:48] Samir Patel: Sounds reasonable. Can we also test a lightweight canonicalizer inserted at the edge? Even a small increase in logical reuse could be huge.
[04:57] Priya Nair: Yes — experiment matrix should include canonicalizer on/off as a factor. So 2x eviction configs x 2x canonicalizer = 4 runs. Each 48h is 8 days total — we can parallelize if we get a second slot.
[05:11] Jordan Lee: We'll try to provision a second test slot. Priya, can you handle orchestration?
[05:16] Priya Nair: Yep, I'll set up the test slots and logs. Need Samir to provide anonymized traces and a couple of representative prompt families.
[05:24] Samir Patel: We'll share the traces and a doc with prompt families. There may be some UI-driven tokenization oddities.
[05:31] Rachel Gomez: Also, we want fallback behavior documented. If cache is saturated, what is graceful degradation? Prefer fallback to smaller but faster model rather than failing open.
[05:40] Maya Chen: Redwood can policy-route to a lower-capacity model variant if the primary returns capacity errs or latency spikes. We can demo the routing rule.
[05:47] Liam O'Connor: From security/compliance — routing to other model variants is okay as long as logging/audit is preserved and encryption in transit is maintained. Also want RBAC for who can change eviction config.
[05:57] Jordan Lee: We'll include RBAC gating in the rollout plan.
[06:00] [longer section omitted — mid-call technical dive and some cross-talk]
[21:15] Priya Nair: Looking at the sample trace you shared, there's a heavy cluster of prompts at midnight UTC — likely background batch jobs creating noise. We should drop those from the cache experiments or isolate them.
[21:27] Samir Patel: Ah yeah, that's our ETL job hitting the same model for data normalization. We'll exclude those from the pilot window.
[21:33] Maya Chen: Good catch. That ETL would artificially inflate cold-starts if included.
[21:38] Priya Nair: Also, we instrumented a small metric to detect prompt-stem similarity using a Jaccard-ish token overlap. If overlap > 0.7, we treat as same prefix for cache key. It increased simulated hit rate from 48% to 61% in another customer. Could help here.
[21:54] Rachel Gomez: That sounds promising. How brittle is that approach with synonyms and paraphrase?
[21:59] Priya Nair: It's brittle for paraphrase; it's a quick win for templated prompts. For paraphrase we recommend a lightweight semantic hashing step, but that's higher cost.
[22:07] Samir Patel: We can start with the token overlap method — low friction.
[22:11] Jordan Lee: Great. About instrumentation — we need the following metrics for each run: prefix_hit_rate, kv_hit_rate, tokens_generated, p50_latency, p95_latency, error_rate, memory_usage, and cost estimate. Priya will add logging hooks.
[22:27] Priya Nair: We'll push an agent that emits those metrics every minute.
[22:32] Jordan Lee: Anything else from the Bluefield side?
[22:35] Nadia Ruiz: Business question — what's a success threshold for this pilot? We want cost/token reduction > 20% without p95 latency increase > 15% and prefix hit > 60%. Is that realistic?
[22:47] Priya Nair: That's ambitious but feasible with canonicalization plus adaptive retention. We'll validate in the runs.
[22:54] Jordan Lee: Okay, we'll treat that as the success metric.
[22:58] [wrap-up and recap]
[23:05] Jordan Lee: Recap: Samir provides traces + prompt families (anonymized) by 2025-08-07. Jordan will share KV tuning doc and canonicalizer example by 2025-08-08. Priya will spin test slots and run the 4-run matrix with or without canonicalizer, target baseline run on 2025-08-11. We'll aim to have results and a short readout next week.
[23:28] Samir Patel: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[23:33] Rachel Gomez: Thanks.
[23:35] Liam O'Connor: Thanks all.
[23:38] Jordan Lee: Great — adjourn.

(timestamps late in the call are approximate; transcription includes some mis-hears and auto-caption errors like "K-V cash" and "Redwood Dedicate")
